title: Ashʿarite Occasionalism — does fire make cotton burn?
when: The Ashʿarite school took shape around al-Ashʿarī (c. 873–935) in the ninth–tenth centuries. Al-Ghazālī (c. 1055–1111) revisited causation in The Incoherence of the Philosophers (c. 1095); how strongly he endorsed occasionalism remains debated.
people: Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, al-Ghazālī, and Avicenna, whose account of natural causes became a central interlocutor.
origin: Abbasid-era Iraq, especially Basra and Baghdad, in kalām debates over divine omnipotence, human agency, and Greek-influenced philosophy.
idea: On an occasionalist account, God alone is the ultimate creator of events; created things do not independently necessitate their effects. Al-Ghazālī’s example: fire touches cotton, and burning follows, but repeated conjunction does not prove a necessary connection. God creates the burning on that occasion, within the world’s regular customary order, and could produce a different outcome—leaving room for miracles. This does not mean nature is unpredictable or that humans cannot act: Ashʿarite theologians used kasb (“acquisition”) to explain human responsibility while affirming divine sovereignty. Scholars still debate whether al-Ghazālī rejected all creaturely causation or only the claim that natural causes necessitate their effects.
relevance: The view distinguishes reliable regularity from metaphysical necessity: a pattern may be stable without being unavoidable. That distinction still informs debates about laws of nature, causation, miracles, and scientific explanation. It also leaves a live challenge: if effects depend on divine action rather than the powers of things, how should we understand responsibility and the causal structure of ordinary life?

sources.name: Causation in Arabic and Islamic Thought — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
